title: Building a model of the molecular interactions of fertilization
text:
At the molecular level, our understanding of the recognition, adhesion, and fusion between sperm and egg to
form an embryo is limited. This presents challenges for diagnosing the causes of infertility and limits the
success of assisted reproductive technologies. C. elegans is an ideal system for the unbiased discovery of
genes and proteins required for reproductive processes and for investigating the interactions and
interdependence of these proteins to build mechanistic models of the processes of fertilization.

title: Role of a novel human mast cell G protein coupled receptor in Allergy and Inflammation
text:
Mast cells are important for allergic and inflammatory disorders including asthma and psoriasis. Although mice
have been used to study these diseases, the target receptor present in mouse mast cells is different from the
one found in human mast cells. We developed new animal models expressing the human receptor, which
provides new preclinical models to study the mechanisms involved in asthma and psoriasis.

title: Multi-Disciplinary Training Program in Cardiovascular Imaging at Stanford
text:
With the rise in the impact of cardiovascular disease on U.S. and world health, and the rapid advances in imaging
technologies and cardiovascular biology, it is critical to train the next generation of investigators in technology-
based cardiovascular imaging research. Stanford University has world-class faculty, the necessary resources,
and the collaborative milieu to address the major public health problem of cardiovascular disease. This
multidisciplinary T32 training program in Cardiovascular Imaging at Stanford (CVIS) is designed to train
postdoctoral fellows in clinical, engineering, and molecular imaging technology, and to foster their development
into investigators dedicated to identifying innovative solutions and capable of translating basic research into
clinical success to combat cardiovascular diseases.

title: Realizing BRAVE-EM for Nanoscale Multicolor Imaging in Biology: Biological Real-space Absorption Visualization by photoEmission Electron Microscopy
text:
Human disease is inherently heterogenous, and every cell in a person’s body has a
different protein expression, presentation of antigens, and structural environment. The
proposed research aims to develop microscopy techniques that will allow us to
reconstruct not only the three-dimensional structural network of cells and tissues in
biological material such as tumors, but also the 3D variation in molecular expression,
simultaneously. Such techniques will ultimately allow us to determine how cells and tissue
work, or fail to work, cooperatively in the progression of diseases such as cancer and
identify new opportunities for treatment.

title: Examining the role of dCA2 sharp wave ripple dynamics and neural activity in social memory and attachment
text:
Neuronal activity in the hippocampal CA2 region is required for social recognition memory, the loss of which is
detrimental to mental health. Here, I will investigate the role of CA2 activity during social interaction and
subsequent memory consolidation events during the development of social attachments. This proposal will
expand our fundamental understanding of regions and regional activity important for forming and remembering
social relationships, thus paving the way for possible therapies for deficits in social memory and bonding.

title: The role of myosin binding protein-C S-glutathionylation and phosphorylation on diastolic dysfunction in the diabetic heart
text:
Prolongation of the heart’s relaxation phase is a hallmark of diabetic heart disease and a major public health
concern given the high incidence of type II diabetes mellitus. Sarcomere proteins help to regulate relaxation
parameters of the heart, and their modification might serve as a new target to treat diastolic dysfunction in the
diabetic heart. This proposal aims to uncover new molecular mechanisms that link the S-glutathionylation and
phosphorylation of cardiac myosin binding protein-C to better understand the role of sarcomere proteins in
modulating relaxation of the diabetic heart.

title: Harnessing Trained Immunity as a Radiation Medical Countermeasure
text:
Exposure to radiation from a nuclear explosion or medical use will cause immune system deficiencies and long-
lasting complications due to loss of natural immune balance that is needed for protection from infectious diseases
and cancer. This project will advance development of using natural immune system enhancing stimulants called
CpG-DNA to regenerate bone marrow recovery after radiation or radiation with combined traumatic injury.
Studies are designed to optimize translational methods for using CpG-DNA as a medical countermeasure
improve recovery from radiation exposure and trauma.

title: Human Genetics and Phenotyping Core
text: This core is central for all experiments in this program project and capitalizes on the Pakistan Genomic Resource (PGR) that has established the largest biobank of “Human Knockouts”. Specifically, PGR has leveraged high levels of consanguinity in Pakistan and has conducted whole-exome and whole-genome sequencing studies in 80,000 participants and has already identified complete KOs for >5000 genes and heterozygous KOs for >18,000 genes. PGR has also found rare homozygotes for many missense variants, many of which have now been characterized to be loss of function (LoF) or gain of function (GoF). Moreover, PGR has also recruited > 45,000 cases with myocardial infarction, > 20,000 cases with echo-confirmed heart failure, > 6,000 cases with imaging confirmed stroke – all of these participants have undergone genotyping for GWAS and whole-exome sequencing studies. Services that will be provided by the core will include: (i) for high priority genes across the four projects, deep phenotyping of KOs / mutant probands and their consanguineous family members. Such phenotyping studies will include: detailed clinical exams, electrocardiograms (ECGs) and echocardiograms, assessment of any rhythm disorders through Biotel patch heart monitors, exercise stress test, and detailed biochemical exams; (ii) analyses of large-scale genomic data in relation to cardiovascular traits and outcomes (i.e., myocardial infarction, stroke, heart failure, ECG traits and other risk factors) recorded in PGR, UKBiobank and other population-based resources in up to 1 million participants.

title: Modeling and Characterization of NAFLD Phenotypes in a Severely Affected Family
text:
The proposed research is directly relevant to public health because it will quantify and analyze novel
genes for the study of non-alcoholic fatty liver disease. Because this project makes use of translational
methods in laboratory-engineered human liver tissue with direct relevance to development of therapeutic
targets for a widely prevalent liver disease, this project is directly relevant to development of human therapies
to the NIH mission to enhance health, lengthen life, and reduce the burdens of illness and disability.

title: Mild Cognitive Impairment: A Prospective Community Study
text: Mild Cognitive Impairment: A Prospective Community Study. Dementia is a leading cause of disability and death in older adults. Its incidence increases exponentially with age. Identifying independent risk factors and valid disease markers are critical steps towards prevention, improved diagnosis, and treatment. To enhance clinical and public health care, these factors must be identified in population settings. We seek to extend, for a further five years, a 20-year prospective population-based study of mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and dementia in a low SES-area of southwestern Pennsylvania. The original richly characterized cohort is now aged 85+, and at maximum risk for dementia; we have replenished the cohort and enhanced its ethnoracial diversity by recruiting additional participants from a predominantly African American community. Our objective remains to identify, at the population level, risk factors for clinically relevant adverse cognitive outcomes of MCI, cognitive decline, and progression to dementia. During the current award period we have assessed several plasma biomarkers of Alzheimer's disease and related disorders (ADRD), examined data from ultra-high-resolution (7 Tesla) brain MRI scans on cerebrovascular morphology and gray matter volume including hippocampal segments, and reported preliminary GWAS and RNA sequencing results. We have also examined social determinants of health (SDOH) in relation to MCI. Our aims for the next five years are to build on these discoveries. exploring (1) additional novel plasma ADRD biomarkers, (2) additional 7T brain imaging to examine neural markers of aging including arterial tortuosity and white matter volume, hippocampal volume (whole and subfields), neuroplasticity (synapse/dendrite density), (3) whole genome sequencing to (i) to characterize and fine- map the novel candidate loci identified in GWAS analyses, identify additional and full spectrum of common and low-frequency/rare variants influencing cognitive decline; (ii) to identify novel loci using genome-wide genotype and WGS data for new plasma biomarkers, (iii) to functionally characterize the identified significant variants using genomics and bioinformatics approaches; and (4) to examine the associations of plasma biomarkers, 7T imaging markers, and genomics with one another, and how these markers are distributed by race/ethnicity and by SDOH, using state-of-the-art statistical modeling. RELEVANCE (See instructions): This ongoing population-based epidemiologic study of mild cognitive impairment (MCI) is being conducted among older adults in an under-resourced, ethnoracially diverse, group of communities in a Rust Belt region of Pennsylvania. Our purpose is to identify risk factors for MCI and dementia, and biological markers that predict cognitive decline and progression to dementia, so that steps can be taken to lower these risks.

title: Resource Core II: In Vivo Core
text: ABSTRACT – Resource Core II: In Vivo Core The proposed U19, referred to as the CASEPR program, aims to develop robust, durable disease-modifying CRISPR-mediated genomic gene-editing therapies for the neurodegenerative disorders of Huntington’s disease (HD) and C9orf72-associated amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (C9-ALS). These investigations will require preclinical in vivo studies of drug delivery and efficacy. The mission of ‘Resource Core II: In Vivo Core’ is to carry out all of the in vivo non-GLP small animal studies for the research programs supported by this U19. The In Vivo Core will provide essential services necessary to carry out all three research projects in the CASEPR program through the following aims: In Aim 1 the In Vivo Resource Core will perform all of the non-GLP in vivo administration of gene-editing vectors for all CASPER program research projects to achieve optimal dosing and distribution of the CRISPR vectors using convection-enhanced delivery neurosurgical techniques. In Aim 2 we will conduct standardized phenotypic assays in mouse models of disease to assess the efficacy of gene editing on rescue of disease-related behavior. Finally, in Aim 3 In Vivo Core researchers will be responsible for procuring relevant tissues from experimental animals and shipping of materials to the other resource cores, the Genomics Core and the Biological Outcomes Core, as appropriate. Centralizing the in vivo non-GLP small animal work will ensure uniformity in both neurosurgical studies and behavioral assessments across all projects. Research output from the In Vivo Core will provide essential data on investigational drug targeting, distribution, editing efficacy, and behavioral impact. The services provided by the In Vivo Core will accelerate the timeline from preclinical animal studies to IND by consolidation of resources and expertise.

title: Exploring the role of a premotor cell type for active sensor control in Drosophila
text:
The challenge, or advantage, of sensing during movement is as evolutionarily conserved as motile behavior
itself. The experiments proposed here will illuminate fundamental mechanisms of how the nervous system
integrates sensory information with motor plans for movement. By elucidating elementary circuit function in
Drosophila, this research will increase our understanding of how nervous systems use sensory information to
guide coordinated movement and behavior, which is crucial for understanding how these mechanisms fail in
disease.

title: Function and Transcriptional Regulation of Leiomodin1
text:
We discovered a coronary artery disease (CAD) phenotype in mice lacking Leiomodin1 (Lmod1), a cytoskeletal
gene harboring a mutation associated with human CAD. Using the most sophisticated tools available, we will
(a) elucidate the underlying nature of this rare CAD phenotype; (b) elucidate a potential mechanism involving
LMOD1 nucleolar binding to a key transcription factor; and (c) define the transcriptional control of Lmod1 in
mice, including the role of a human CAD-associated mutation. The results will provide informative insight into
the in vivo function and transcriptional regulation of LMOD1, a CAD risk allele of unknown function.

title: Structure and function studies of the orphan cytochrome P450s CYP126A1 and CYP143A1 from the human pathogen Mycobacterium tuberculosis
text:
This research investigates two cytochrome P450 enzymes from Mycobacterium tuberculosis that may play
essential roles in bacterial metabolism and infection. The essential goal of this project is to understand the
structure, function, and inhibition of two orphan P450 enzymes, CYP126A1 and CYP143A1, which are highly
conserved among pathogenic mycobacteria. Insights gained from this research will guide the development of
new therapeutic strategies to combat drug-resistant TB and improve global public health.

title: Preclinical microphysiological tumor models for nuclear medicine
text:
Microphysiological tumor systems, which are small human tumors grown outside the body, are useful models
for cancer research, drug discovery, and personalized therapy, but they lack clinically relevant imaging
endpoints. This project will develop a quantitative and high-resolution approach to image these microtumors
using the existing array of clinical PET radiotracers, thus bridging the gap in physical scale that exist between
clinical tumor imaging and microphysiological tumor models. The approach will be demonstrated in a pilot
study in a cohort of head-and-neck cancer patients.

title: Integrated bioprinting and optogenetics platform for evaluating neural activity in stem cell-derived retinal disease models
text:
Neurodegenerative diseases (including retinal degenerations) contribute a substantial socioeconomic burden
in terms of functional impairment, lost productivity, and associated medical care and treatment. This project
aims to develop a platform technology by integrating 3D bioprinting and opto-neurotechnology to create
brain/retina-on-a-chip" devices toward the diagnosis of neurological disorders.

title: Clinically-calibrated Accelerated Fatigue Test for Predicting the Clinical Performance of Dental Restorative Materials
text:
There is now an urgent need to develop more clinically-relevant tests, or medical device development
tools (MDDT), that are alternatives to clinical studies to help accelerate the translation of new dental
biomaterials. In this biphasic R61/R33 application, we propose a new MDDT in the form of clinically-
calibrated accelerated fatigue and biofilm tests, on a simple yet clinically-representative model
composite restoration. The proposed MDDT is expected to enhance the quality and efficiency of dental
materials evaluation associated with the FDA regulatory review process.

title: Harnessing Microbial-Metabolite Signals to Guide Endoscopic and Transmural Healing for Pediatric Crohn's Disease
text:
Pediatric-onset Crohn’s disease (CD) is a chronic progressive inflammatory gastrointestinal disease with
significant lifelong morbidity and irreversible complications if it is inadequately treated. Microbial factors constitute
an important role in the disease, and while they may impact a patient’s response to medications and are
potentially modifiable via treatment, knowledge about how to best utilize these factors to optimize and
individualize treatment is still unknown. To improve medication selection and dosing decisions, we aim to harness
microbial factors to guide treatment decisions and evaluate the effect of treatment on 1) endoscopic healing and
2) transmural healing (deep healing throughout the bowel) as assessed by noninvasive point-of-care intestinal
ultrasound.

title: Using Novel Machine Learning Methods to Personalize Strategies for Prevention of Persistent AKI after Cardiac Surgery
text:
The strategy to prevent acute kidney injury (AKI) and its progression relies on clinical interventions provided as
a care-bundle to minimize injury to the kidneys. This care-bundle, however, lacks the ability to personalize care
for patients. This project will use novel machine learning methods to determine a personalized strategy for
prevention of persistent AKI after cardiac surgery.

title: Genetic circuitry governing heart growth and repair
text:
This study aims to reveal the physiological triggers of cardiac regenerative potential loss during postnatal
growth. This will provide novel insights into organ regeneration, possibly suggesting new targets and
strategies to treat heart failure.
